calls.title: Pay when it arrives
calls.setup: You sell books online in India, but few Indians use credit cards. Couriers who collect cash for you take weeks to pay you, and they charge high fees.
calls.question: How do you let people pay?

options.label: Offer cash on delivery and build your own delivery team, at a high cost.
options.outcome: Flipkart offered cash on delivery and started its own delivery arm as a pilot in December 2010, because it did not want outside couriers holding its cash. That arm, eKart, later grew to serve over 800 cities.
options.why: Buyers who didn't trust online shopping could see the product before paying, and running delivery yourself meant the cash came back fast.
options.takeaway: If customers don't trust you yet, let them pay after they see the product.

options.label: Offer cash on delivery through couriers, who already reach most of India.
options.outcome: More people buy, but your money sits with the couriers for weeks. The more you sell, the less cash you have in hand.
options.why: You solved the customer's problem but created a cash problem for yourself.
options.better: Offer cash on delivery and run your own delivery, so the cash reaches you fast.
options.takeaway: Fix the customer's problem without creating a cash problem.

options.label: Take only cards and bank transfers, and teach buyers to use them.
options.outcome: Your cash reaches you directly, but most buyers don't trust paying online yet. While you spend years teaching them, your shop grows slowly.
options.why: The real wall was trust, not just cards. Teaching a whole country a new habit is slow, and a rival who takes cash wins those buyers first.
options.better: Let customers pay cash at the door, and build your own delivery so the cash comes back fast.
options.takeaway: Your payment method can decide who becomes a customer.

calls.realHistory: Flipkart offered cash on delivery and began its own delivery arm in December 2010. It later grew to serve over 800 cities.

calls.title: A quarter of the price
calls.setup: You make washing powder at home, while the big brand, Surf, sells at Rs 13 a kilo.
calls.question: How do you price your powder?

options.label: Price it just under Surf, so shoppers see a quality powder.
options.outcome: Shoppers see two powders at almost the same price and pick the famous one. Your powder stays on the shelf.
options.why: Against a famous brand, a slightly lower price gives buyers no real reason to switch.
options.better: Price far below Surf for families who could never afford it, and sell to them directly.
options.takeaway: A new brand needs a clear reason to choose it.

options.label: Sell through shops in your city first, and grow as money comes in.
options.outcome: You build a small, loyal following, but growth is slow, and the shops take a cut of every packet.
options.why: Starting small keeps risk low, but it leaves the huge market below Surf's price for someone faster.
options.better: Go after that huge market directly, with a very low price and door-to-door selling.
options.takeaway: Safe and small can mean someone else takes the big market.

options.label: Price it at Rs 3.50 a kilo, about a quarter of Surf's price, and sell door to door.
options.outcome: The founder priced Nirma at Rs 3.50 a kilo and sold it door to door by bicycle. Nirma became India's largest-selling detergent within a decade, and Surf was badly hurt.
options.why: Millions of families wanted washing powder but could not afford the big brand. You built a product for them.
options.takeaway: A huge market often waits below the big brand's price.

calls.realHistory: Nirma launched at Rs 3.50 a kilo against Surf's Rs 13, sold door to door, and became India's largest-selling detergent within a decade.

sources.label: From selling detergent door-to-door on his bicycle (Business Today, 2023)
Multinational Strategies and Developing Countries (Harvard Business School, 2010)

calls.title: Recall everything?
calls.setup: Seven people near Chicago have died after taking Tylenol capsules that someone had laced with poison. The capsules were sold in Chicago-area stores. Tylenol has 35% of its market.
calls.question: What do you do?

options.label: Recall all Tylenol in the Chicago area, where the poisoned bottles were sold.
options.outcome: You spend less on the recall, but fear doesn't stay in Chicago. Shoppers across the country can't tell safe bottles from bad ones, so they stop buying.
options.why: The poison was found in one city, but the doubt was everywhere. A local recall left every other bottle in question.
options.better: Recall every bottle in the country, and come back with packaging no one can tamper with.
options.takeaway: If buyers can't tell safe from unsafe, a partial fix doesn't remove the doubt.

options.label: Recall every bottle in the country, though the poison was found only near Chicago.
options.outcome: Johnson & Johnson recalled 31 million bottles across the US, at a cost of $100 million. Tylenol's share fell to 7%. After it came back in tamper-proof packaging, it returned to 35% by the end of 1983.
options.why: Only a full recall removed every doubt, and the new sealed packs then gave shoppers a reason to come back.
options.takeaway: Remove the doubt completely, then give buyers a reason to return.

options.label: Warn the public, then wait for the police so you don't spread panic.
options.outcome: While you wait, rumours fill the silence. Shops pull Tylenol on their own, and shoppers learn to buy other brands.
options.why: Fear spreads faster than facts. By waiting, you let the news and the shops decide what happened to your brand.
options.better: Act first and big: recall every bottle, then come back with packaging no one can tamper with.
options.takeaway: In a scare, the company that moves first gets to tell the story.

calls.realHistory: Johnson & Johnson recalled 31 million bottles nationwide and relaunched Tylenol in tamper-proof packaging. Its share fell to 7%, then returned to 35% by the end of 1983.

sources.label: Tylenol and the legacy of J&J's James Burke (Knowledge at Wharton, 2012)

calls.title: Hire school-leavers
calls.setup: Your software company in Chennai needs programmers. Graduates from top colleges get many job offers. Young people straight out of school would need two years of training.
calls.question: How do you find talent?

options.label: Pay more than rivals to win top graduates, who can start work at once.
options.outcome: You hire good people, but salaries keep rising, and many leave when a bigger company offers more.
options.why: Competing on salary alone is a race where the richest company wins.
options.better: Train your own talent from people others overlook.
options.takeaway: Buying talent is expensive. Building it can be cheaper and more loyal.

options.label: Hire outside agencies to write the code, and keep your own team small.
options.outcome: Work gets done and costs stay low, but your best know-how sits with agencies that also work for others. Quality is hard to control.
options.why: For a software company, the people who write the code are the product, so handing that work to others means handing away your future.
options.better: Build your own team, even if it means training people yourself.
options.takeaway: Don't outsource the thing that makes your company special.

options.label: Train school-leavers for two years, and pay them while they learn.
options.outcome: In 2004 the company, then called AdventNet and now Zoho, started what became Zoho University: a two-year course for Class 12 students. Students pay no fees and get Rs 10,000 a month. Most are hired by Zoho, and many come from low-income, often rural, families.
options.why: You found talent where others weren't looking, and trained it the way your company works. Most of them went on to work for you.
options.takeaway: You can train talent instead of buying it.

calls.realHistory: Zoho started Zoho University in 2004, training Class 12 students for two years with a stipend. Most of them go on to work at Zoho.

sources.label: Why did Zoho start a school? (Scroll, 2024)

calls.title: Shampoo for small change
calls.setup: Shampoo is mostly sold in bottles. One brand already sells small packets at Rs 2 each. You have a new shampoo to launch.
calls.question: How do you sell your shampoo?

options.label: Sell single-use packets at a very low price, mostly in village shops.
options.outcome: The founder's company, then called Beauty Products and later renamed CavinKare, launched Chik shampoo in 10 ml packets in 1983, at a very low price, and pushed it in rural markets. Within a couple of years Chik became the top shampoo in South India.
options.why: You made the product fit what customers could pay each day, not what the big brands wanted to sell.
options.takeaway: Make the pack small enough for the customer's pocket.

options.label: Sell bottles like the big brands, and spend on ads to look as good.
options.outcome: You fight the big brands on their own ground, with much less money. Shops give you little space, and few buyers switch.
options.why: Copying the leader's pack and price gives poorer buyers no new reason to try you.
options.better: Make a pack small enough for the customer's pocket.
options.takeaway: Don't fight the leader on the leader's terms.

options.label: Sell smaller, cheaper bottles in towns, where more people can buy them.
options.outcome: A few more people can afford it, but a bottle is still too much for many families. You miss the villages and small towns.
options.why: Smaller helped, but not small enough for the biggest group of buyers.
options.better: Go all the way down to a single-use packet at a tiny price, sold in rural shops.
options.takeaway: Close to affordable is not affordable.

calls.realHistory: Chik launched 10 ml shampoo packets in 1983 at a very low price and became South India's top shampoo within a couple of years.

sources.label: The man behind the sachet revolution in India (Madras Musings, 2021)

calls.title: Sell cereal to stay alive
calls.setup: Your startup lets people stay in strangers' homes. Investor after investor has said no, and the business needs money to survive.
calls.question: What do you do?

options.label: Keep going on your credit cards, so you give away no part of the company.
options.outcome: You survive a few more months, but the debt grows, and you still have nothing new to show investors.
options.why: Debt buys time but does not show anyone why they should believe in you.
options.better: Raise cash in a way that also shows your grit and creativity.
options.takeaway: Buying time is not the same as building proof.

options.label: Make and sell novelty cereal boxes for cash, though it isn't your business.
options.outcome: The founders designed and sold election-themed cereal boxes at $40 each and raised about $30,000. The hustle impressed the startup programme Y Combinator, which accepted them and invested $20,000.
options.why: You kept the company alive and showed investors exactly the kind of grit they look for.
options.takeaway: Showing grit can win your first backers.

options.label: Change the idea to one investors like more, such as a hotel booking site.
options.outcome: Investors listen more, but now you are one more booking site against big rivals. The thing that made you different is gone.
options.why: Investors saying no doesn't mean the idea is bad, because many good ideas look strange at first. By dropping yours, you became ordinary.
options.better: Find a creative way to raise a little cash and keep going long enough to prove the idea.
options.takeaway: Early rejection doesn't always mean the idea is wrong.

calls.realHistory: Airbnb's founders sold election-themed cereal boxes at $40 each, raised about $30,000, and won a place and $20,000 from Y Combinator.

sources.label: Airbnb's CEO says a $40 cereal box changed the course of the company (Fortune, 2023)

calls.title: Quartz only
calls.setup: A government-owned company rules India's watch market, mainly with mechanical watches that need winding. Quartz watches are a newer technology.
calls.question: What kind of watches do you make?

options.label: Make only quartz watches, though most buyers still wear mechanical ones.
options.outcome: Titan, a joint venture of Tata and TIDCO, a Tamil Nadu government agency, made only quartz watches. Its first range sold at Rs 350 to 900. The old leader, HMT, went into slow decline, and Titan held over 60% of India's organised watch market by 2012.
options.why: You built for where the technology was going, not where it had been.
options.takeaway: When technology is changing, build for the new thing, not the old one.

options.label: Make mechanical watches, the kind most Indian buyers wear today.
options.outcome: You become a smaller copy of the leader, just as buyers start moving to quartz.
options.why: Copying the leader's technology means you arrive late, just as the market changes.
options.better: Build only for the new technology, quartz.
options.takeaway: Don't copy the leader's past.

options.label: Make both kinds, so you're covered whichever way buyers move.
options.outcome: You cover both markets, but your quartz watches don't stand out, and your mechanical ones fade.
options.why: Covering both sides lowers the risk of choosing wrong, but it splits your effort just as the market moves.
options.better: Commit fully to quartz and be the best at it.
options.takeaway: Half a bet on the future is often a weak bet.

calls.realHistory: Titan launched in 1987 with quartz watches only, against a leader that mainly made mechanical ones. By 2012 Titan held over 60% of India's organised watch market.

calls.title: Worms in the chocolate
calls.setup: It is October 2003. Worms have been found in your chocolates in Maharashtra. At first you defended your factory and said you could not watch every shop. The regulator moved to prosecute, and sales are falling.
calls.question: What do you do now?

options.label: Prove your factory is clean, and work with shops to store chocolate better.
options.outcome: You may be right about the shops, but parents don't read factory reports. They keep away, and the story stays in the news.
options.why: Even if you are right, a report doesn't make a parent feel safe. Buyers needed to see a change they could hold in their hands.
options.better: Fix the part you control, like the packaging, and show customers the fix.
options.takeaway: In a crisis, being right is not enough. Customers need to see you act.

options.label: Cut prices for a few months, so worried buyers have a reason to return.
options.outcome: Some buyers come back for the discount, but the worry stays. When prices go back up, they leave again.
options.why: A discount fixes price, but the problem was trust.
options.better: Fix the packaging and show people how you make your chocolate.
options.takeaway: Don't answer a trust problem with a discount.

options.label: Pay for new packaging and ads that show how the chocolate is made.
options.outcome: Cadbury improved its packaging and ran ads in which a famous film star visited the factory. Sales, which had fallen after the news, recovered.
options.why: You fixed what you could control and let customers see it for themselves.
options.takeaway: In a crisis, fix the problem and show the fix.

calls.realHistory: Cadbury first defended its factory standards and said it could not watch every shop. It then improved its packaging and ran an ad campaign showing its factory, and sales recovered.

sources.label: Previous food and beverage scares in India (The National, 2015)

calls.title: Answer the cheap rival
calls.setup: You make Surf, India's leading washing powder. A cheap new powder called Nirma is winning huge numbers of customers who never bought Surf, and now some who did.
calls.question: How do you respond?

options.label: Keep focusing on Surf, since most of Nirma's buyers were never your customers.
options.outcome: Nirma keeps growing, and by the time you act, it is the biggest name in the market.
options.why: Cheap rivals start with buyers you don't want, then move up to the ones you do.
options.better: Launch your own low-price brand early, and keep Surf as the premium one.
options.takeaway: Never dismiss a cheap rival because its first customers aren't yours.

options.label: Launch your own cheap brand, even if it takes some sales from Surf.
options.outcome: Hindustan Lever launched a low-cost brand, Wheel, to fight Nirma. But its answer came only after a long delay. The shock changed how Unilever sold in poorer markets, including selling small packets.
options.why: A second, cheaper brand let you fight on price without cutting Surf's. The mistake was waiting so long.
options.takeaway: When a cheap rival attacks, fight with a second brand, and fight early.

options.label: Cut Surf's price to match, and use your size to win the price war.
options.outcome: You win some buyers back, but your profits fall, and Surf starts to look ordinary.
options.why: Cutting the price of your premium brand damages it to fight a battle it wasn't built for.
options.better: Fight with a separate cheaper brand, and keep Surf premium.
options.takeaway: Don't cheapen your best brand to fight a price war.

calls.realHistory: Hindustan Lever answered Nirma with a low-cost brand, Wheel, but only after a long delay. The lesson shaped Unilever's later push into small packets for poorer markets.

sources.label: Multinational Strategies and Developing Countries (Harvard Business School, 2010)
Hindustan Unilever: how the FMCG giant tailored itself for India (Forbes India, 2024)

calls.title: The small fish buys the big fish
calls.setup: Tata Tea grows tea and wants to grow abroad. Its first try to buy the British brand Tetley, the world's second-biggest tea company, failed for lack of money. Now there is another chance.
calls.question: What do you do?

options.label: Borrow heavily to buy Tetley, a company much bigger than you.
options.outcome: In 2000 Tata Tea bought Tetley for £271 million, a deal funded largely by borrowing. Tetley became Tata's main global brand, and about two-thirds of Tata Tea's sales later came from the Tetley Group.
options.why: You bought a global brand that would have taken years to build yourself.
options.takeaway: Borrowing to buy a brand can work if the brand can earn enough to repay the loan.

options.label: Buy more tea gardens, the business you already know best.
options.outcome: You grow more tea, but you stay a seller of raw tea while others earn the brand profits.
options.why: More gardens make you bigger in the low-profit part of the business.
options.better: Move into brands, where the profits are.
options.takeaway: Growing bigger in the wrong part of the business is not growth.

options.label: Build your own tea brand abroad, step by step, with no big loan.
options.outcome: You grow abroad step by step, but it takes many years and a lot of advertising to become known.
options.why: Building a global brand from zero is slow and costly.
options.better: Buy a famous brand that can earn enough to repay the loan.
options.takeaway: Sometimes buying a brand is faster than building one.

calls.realHistory: Tata Tea bought Tetley in 2000 for £271 million, mostly with borrowed money. Tetley became its main global brand.

calls.title: Close every store for training
calls.setup: It is early 2008. Your company believes Starbucks has lost its way in its US stores. Your returning CEO has a plan that includes better staff training.
calls.question: How do you retrain thousands of baristas?

options.label: Send new training videos to every store, so no store loses a sale.
options.outcome: Busy staff watch them between orders, and service stays the same.
options.why: Busy staff can't learn much between orders, and a turnaround needs a moment that everyone can see.
options.better: Invest real time in training, together, so the change sticks.
options.takeaway: Training squeezed between orders rarely changes how people work.

options.label: Retrain staff in small groups over months, with no store closed.
options.outcome: Staff get trained, but slowly, and customers see little change.
options.why: Quiet training works, but a turnaround also needs everyone to see that you are serious.
options.better: Make one big, visible move that shows staff and customers quality comes first.
options.takeaway: In a turnaround, people need to see the change, not just hear about it.

options.label: Close every US store for one evening to retrain everyone, and lose those sales.
options.outcome: On 26 February 2008, Starbucks closed nearly 7,100 US stores for one evening to retrain baristas. Many called it a gimmick. Starbucks also closed about 600 weak US stores, and its profit fell sharply that year. By 2010 it posted record results, after a turnaround that included much more than the training evening.
options.why: Closing every store showed staff and customers that quality mattered more than one night of sales.
options.takeaway: Your people are the product, so invest in their skills.

calls.realHistory: Starbucks closed nearly 7,100 US stores for one evening in February 2008 to retrain baristas, as part of a wider turnaround that led to record results in 2010.

sources.label: Starbucks closes 7,100 stores for training (Retail Customer Experience, 2008)

calls.title: From energy drink to aam panna
calls.setup: Your company sells a cheap energy drink, Tzinga, at Rs 25 against Red Bull's Rs 95. One day a co-founder brings aam panna to work, and it gives the team an idea.
calls.question: What do you bet on next?

options.label: Launch fruit juices, a big market that buyers already know.
options.outcome: You get on the shelf, but your juices look like everyone else's.
options.why: Copying the big brands' products gives shoppers no reason to choose you.
options.better: Bottle the traditional Indian drinks people grew up with.
options.takeaway: Different beats slightly cheaper.

options.label: Bottle traditional drinks like aam panna, an untested idea.
options.outcome: Hector Beverages launched Paper Boat drinks in Delhi and Bengaluru in August 2013, in pouches that cost less to make than cartons. By 2015 Paper Boat made about 90% of the company's sales.
options.why: You sold something customers already loved but couldn't buy in shops.
options.takeaway: Sell what customers already love but can't find in shops.

options.label: Put your money behind Tzinga, the drink you already sell.
options.outcome: Sales rise a little, but you are still fighting giants in a market they own.
options.why: More ads for a drink like the giants' rarely beat a famous brand.
options.better: Sell something customers love but can't find in shops.
options.takeaway: Don't outspend giants. Out-think them.

calls.realHistory: Hector Beverages launched Paper Boat's traditional Indian drinks in August 2013. Within two years they made about 90% of its sales.

calls.title: Say no to investor money
calls.setup: Your low-cost online share trading company, founded in 2010, made a profit in its second year. You could raise money from investors to grow faster.
calls.question: How do you pay for growth?

options.label: Take investor money and spend big on ads to win the market first.
options.outcome: You grow faster, but now you answer to investors who want even faster growth, and costs climb.
options.why: Investor money speeds things up, but it brings pressure that a profitable company may not need.
options.better: If customers already pay you well, grow from your own profits and keep control.
options.takeaway: Money from investors is not free; it comes with their goals.

options.label: Take a bank loan to grow faster, and keep full ownership.
options.outcome: You grow, but loan payments eat into your profits every month, and one bad year could hurt badly.
options.why: Debt lets you keep ownership, but it adds fixed payments to a business that already pays for itself.
options.better: Grow from the profits you already make.
options.takeaway: Don't add risk you don't need.

options.label: Grow only from profits and keep ads small, even if rivals grow faster.
options.outcome: Zerodha stayed bootstrapped and avoided big ad spending, because its founder did not want to answer to investors. In 2023-24 it made a profit of about Rs 4,700 crore on Rs 8,320 crore of revenue, still without outside investors.
options.why: A profitable business that customers love can fund its own growth and keep control.
options.takeaway: If customers pay you well, you may not need investors.

calls.realHistory: Zerodha never took outside investment. By 2023-24 it made about Rs 4,700 crore in profit.

calls.title: The 10-minute promise
calls.setup: Food delivery is a race for speed, and you could promise food in 10 minutes. It would get attention, but it would cost money to run every day, whether orders come or not.
calls.question: What do you do?

options.label: Test 10-minute delivery with a few customers, even if a rival launches first.
options.outcome: You learn what each fast order really costs before anyone knows, and you only grow it if it makes money.
options.why: A small test shows you the real costs before you commit to a big launch.
options.takeaway: Test the money before you announce the promise.

options.label: Announce 10-minute delivery and try it in one city, to grab attention first.
options.outcome: Zomato announced Zomato Instant in March 2022 and tried it in Gurugram, saying riders would not be punished for late orders. But daily orders were too low to cover the fixed costs. By February 2023 it was relaunched as Zomato Everyday, home-style meals from Rs 89.
options.why: A bold promise got headlines, but daily orders were too low to cover the fixed costs of running it.
options.better: Test quietly with a few users and prove each order can make money before making big promises.
options.takeaway: A big promise must also make money on each order.

options.label: Promise 20 to 30 minutes instead, so you can deliver on time every time.
options.outcome: You keep the promise easily, but it is close to what customers already get, so few switch to you for it.
options.why: A realistic promise is easy to keep, but it gives customers no new reason to choose you.
options.better: Test a faster option quietly, and only promise it when the numbers work.
options.takeaway: Promise what you can keep, and test the rest.

calls.realHistory: Zomato launched 10-minute delivery in 2022, but orders were too low to cover costs, and in 2023 it relaunched the service as Zomato Everyday.

sources.label: Zomato launches rebranded meal service Zomato Everyday (Inc42, 2023)
